one_liner: Header-only C++17 enum reflection (to_string, cast, iteration, bitflags); author-measured builds up to 6.4x faster than magic_enum with default settings.
what_it_does: Gives enum-to-string, string-to-enum, enum-to-index, iteration over values, names and pairs, bitflag handling and enum-indexed containers (enchantum::array, enchantum::bitset) for unmodified enums, with no macros at the declaration. The API mirrors magic_enum's ideas but not its names: enchantum::to_string(e) returns a string_view, enchantum::cast<E>("Name") and index_to_enum return std::optional, and ranges are set with ENCHANTUM_MIN_RANGE/ENCHANTUM_MAX_RANGE or an enum_traits specialization. Adapters exist for iostream, std::format, fmt, nlohmann_json and Quill, and on a C++26 compiler it switches to standard reflection (std::meta) with no range limit.
how_it_is_fast: Like magic_enum it reads enumerator names out of __PRETTY_FUNCTION__ / __FUNCSIG__, but magic_enum instantiates one is_valid<E, V>() / n<V>() function template per candidate value in the range, while enchantum instantiates a single var_name<V0, V1, ..., Vn>() whose signature string lists the whole range at once; a constexpr linear parser (parse_string) then separates named values ('E::Name') from casts ('(E)42'). Fewer template instantiations is where the compile-time and object-size gap comes from. Names are packed into one char array with a uint8/uint16 offset table, which keeps object files small.
when_to_use: Projects with many reflected enums where magic_enum shows up in build profiles; the README's 200-enum GCC case went from 47 s to 8.2 s with default settings.

Enums with values within a few hundred of zero, or wider ranges that magic_enum cannot handle in reasonable time (Large Range -1024..1024: 34 s on GCC with defaults, magic_enum did not finish in 20 minutes).
Third-party or C enums you cannot edit, where simple_enum would need first/last markers added to the enum.
Builds that care about object and executable size: Clang objects 2.7x to 15.6x smaller than magic_enum in the README cases.
Teams that want a compile error when an enum is only partly reflected (the default out-of-bounds check) instead of silently missing values.
when_not_to_use: Wide-string names: the README lists no wchar_t support, which magic_enum has.
Enums with tight known bounds where you can annotate first/last: simple_enum compiled faster in the README's Ideal Range case on all three compilers (GCC 2.7 vs 3.0 s, MSVC 4.7 vs 5.8 s).
MSVC with default settings on small-range enums: Ideal Range is 16 s vs magic_enum 17.9 s, essentially parity.
Forward-declared enums (static_assert), unnamed enums outside MSVC, unscoped enums nested in class templates on Clang, and scoped or aliased enums in templates on NVC++ (docs/limitations.md).
If you need a runtime lookup speedup: only compile time and binary size were measured, no to_string or cast throughput.

integration.form: header-only (CMake target enchantum::enchantum, or the single_include amalgamation)
integration.dependencies: none; optional adapter headers for fmt, std::format, nlohmann_json and Quill
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; GCC 9+, Clang 8+, MSVC 19.24+ (VS 16.4) per README CI list; ICX 2021.1.2+ and NVC++ 22.7+ checked only on godbolt; C++26 reflection path when std::meta is available
integration.platforms: any platform with those compilers; relies on compiler-specific __PRETTY_FUNCTION__/__FUNCSIG__ formats until C++26
integration.thread_safety: not documented; lookups read inline constexpr tables, so there is no shared mutable state in the code read
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same idea as magic_enum but different names (to_string vs enum_name, cast vs enum_cast), different default range (-256..256 vs magic_enum's -128..127), enum_traits specialization instead of magic_enum::customize::enum_range, no wide strings

gotchas: The README's bold compile times are with ENCHANTUM_CHECK_OUT_OF_BOUNDS_BY=0, a define benchmarks/gen.py does not write, and they come from 2025 commits (MSVC column refreshed 2025-06-08, GCC 2025-07-10); the parenthesised default-setting numbers were remeasured on 2026-05-13 after the check was made cheaper (GCC Small 9.3 to 8.2 s, MSVC Large Range 265.1 to 111.4 s), and the check was changed again on 2026-09-07 without a README update. One table therefore mixes library versions and dates, competitor versions are unstated, and Clang Ideal Range moved from 3.5 to 3.8 s across that remeasurement, so differences under about 10% are noise.

gen.py gives simple_enum two extra enumerators, first and last, set to the whole reflection range (the README admits this misuses simple_enum), and gives magic_enum the same range as enchantum. The Small case (-128..128) is essentially magic_enum's documented default (-128..127), so Small (7.8x with the check off, 5.7x default on GCC) is the fair headline; Big and Large Range push magic_enum to 2x and 8x its default range.

The default check rescans [2*min, min-1] and [max+1, 2*max] and static_asserts if an enumerator sits there; values beyond twice the range are still silently dropped, and the check is skipped for bitflag enums and for enums with a specialized enum_traits. Bitflag enums reflect only 0 and single powers of two, not combinations.

Issue #18 (closed): with MSVC /GL and /Ot, string-to-enum cast on a uint8_t enum returned 86 instead of 2 in Release builds; the reporter says magic_enum shows the same, and the page shows no linked fix. Range macros must be identical in every translation unit to avoid ODR violations (docs/limitations.md). The GCC parser stores each name length in a uint8_t and scans at most 255 characters for the separator, so very long enumerator names are outside what it handles (code reading, not tested).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick enchantum over simple_enum (the catalogued sibling that also beats magic_enum on instantiation time) when the enums are not yours to annotate with first/last or when object size matters (simple_enum's Clang objects were 4x to 358x larger in the README cases); pick simple_enum when you can give tight bounds and want the fastest compile. The serialization siblings (Cista++, YAS, bitsery, struct_pack and others) solve a different problem and can use enchantum for enum names.
verified_claims_summary: The author generated translation units with benchmarks/gen.py (200 enums of 16 members, 32 of 200, 200 of 16 at -1024..1024, 100 of 50 at 0..50), each calling to_string once per enum, and averaged 10 compiles with GCC 14.2.0 and Clang 20.1.2 at -O3 and MSVC 19.44 at /Ox on an unnamed Windows 10 machine: with default settings enchantum is 5.7x faster than magic_enum on GCC Small (8.2 vs 47 s), 6.4x on Big, 2.3x on Ideal Range for GCC and Clang, and near parity on MSVC Ideal Range, and with the check disabled 7.8x on GCC Small and Big; Clang object files are 2.7x (Small) to 15.6x (Big) smaller. First-party, compile time and size only.
status_note: Actively maintained (version 0.5.0 prepared 2026-09-07, last commit 2026-09-16, C++26 reflection backend added 2026-08-29), MIT-licensed and header-only, so it is easy to vendor; two open issues (package-manager integration, C++14 support).
